summary_html: An intake **screen** is elevated to a formal **investigation/assessment** under state criteria. CAPTA and CFSR establish the federal expectations for screening, timelines, and investigative quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening/investigation conditions for funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review framework

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that official and vicarious official immunity protect county child-protection employees only for duties requiring judgment or discretion and not for ministerial tasks, affirming as modified with partial summary judgment for the county.
key_cases.relevance: It draws the line between discretionary screening and investigative judgment, which is immune, and ministerial handling of information, which is not.
key_cases.quote: Official immunity only shields government officials from liability stemming from the performance of duties that require the exercise of judgment or discretion

key_cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a Minnesota father's § 1983 claims, holding that a CHIPS petition filed two days after removal followed by a hearing within ten days supplied all the procedural process he was due.
key_cases.relevance: It measures the constitutional adequacy of a Minnesota county's investigation and escalation practices against the shocks-the-conscience standard.
key_cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and reinstating a wrongful-death complaint, the court held that a common-law negligence action may be maintained against a county and its child-protection workers for negligence in the investigation of, and intervention in, reports of suspected child abuse required under the Child Abuse Reporting Act.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Minnesota case on what a county owes a child after intake escalates to investigation, arising from four separate reports the county visited and closed without protective action.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we hold that a cause of action can be maintained for negligence in the investigation of child abuse and neglect reports as required under CARA.

timeline_requirements.deadline: Except in a noncaregiver human trafficking assessment: immediately if sexual abuse or substantial child endangerment is alleged; within 5 calendar days for all other screened in reports
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260E.20, subd. 2(b) sets the face-to-face contact deadline for the local welfare agency.
timeline_requirements.extension_grounds: Face-to-face contact on a report alleging sexual abuse or substantial child endangerment may be postponed for no more than five calendar days if the child is residing in a location confirmed to restrict contact with the alleged offender, or if the local welfare agency is pursuing a court order for the caregiver to produce the child for questioning under Minn. Stat. § 260E.22, subd. 5 (§ 260E.20, subd. 2(b)).

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260E.24, subd. 1 requires the local welfare agency to conclude the assessment or investigation within 45 days.
timeline_requirements.extension_grounds: Only to complete a criminal investigation or to receive expert information requested within 45 days of receipt of the report (Minn. Stat. § 260E.24, subd. 1).
